description:
Around the year 1000, the astronomer Ibn Yunus worked in Cairo on a zij: a book of tables that told you where the Sun, Moon and planets would be on any given day. It turned years of watching the sky into something people could actually use.

We're doing the same thing in 48 hours, with satellites doing the watching.

We're students from Alexandria STEM School, one of Egypt's selective science and engineering high schools. We build real, working tools on NASA data, not slide decks.
summary:
NASA has recorded Earth's active fires since 2000, but with two instruments that cannot be compared directly: MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012). Over Egypt's Nile Delta, VIIRS reports 11 to 20 times more fire pixels than MODIS, so the joined record shows burning jump tenfold in 2012. The fires didn't change; the satellite did. As MODIS retires, the years before 2012 risk becoming unusable.

Zij turns both records into one burning-activity calendar, from November 2000 to today. A model fitted per area on the years both sensors flew converts the MODIS years into VIIRS units. Tested on years it never saw, its season error falls from 77% to 14% (25% when predicting later years), and to 7% in the Nile Delta (10% for later years). Every converted value carries its margin of error.

Draw any area in Egypt, Portugal or Argentina, pick a day or a date range, and Zij tells you in plain words whether this season is normal, with every fire on NASA imagery. Every number can be downloaded and reproduced from NASA FIRMS data.
details:
The problem

NASA's active-fire record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS sees far more small fires: over the Nile Delta in September to November, Suomi NPP reports 11 to 20 times as many fire pixels as Aqua in most years, and 42 times as many in 2018. Joined as they are, the records show burning explode in 2012. A fixed multiplier cannot fix it, because the gap changes with fire size and from year to year. With MODIS retiring, fire managers risk losing the years before 2012.

How it works

  1. Keep real fires. Vegetation fires only; gas flares, industry and weak detections are removed. 6.28 million detections are kept.
  2. One grid. A 0.1 degree cell with at least one fire on a day counts once, so one coarse MODIS pixel and many fine VIIRS pixels weigh the same.
  3. Each satellite. Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are counted separately and averaged within each sensor, so a new satellite never creates a jump. A week inside a satellite outage is "no data", never zero.
  4. Learn the bridge. On 2012 to 2020, when both sensors flew, a model per area learns how MODIS relates to VIIRS: by month, by fire size, and in quiet years.
  5. One record. 2000 to 2011 are converted to VIIRS units, and every converted value carries its error band. Where an area has too little data, Zij says so instead of guessing.

Does it work?

We tested every model on years it never saw: leaving each year out in turn, and predicting 2021 to 2025 from a fit that stops in 2020. Season error is 76.5% for raw MODIS, 24.1% with one fixed multiplier, and 14.2% with Zij (25.2% on the later years). In the Nile Delta it is 6.9%. A clean rebuild from the raw FIRMS files reproduces every published number (REBUILD.md in the repository).

What you can do with it

  • Choose one of 10 preset areas, or draw any box or polygon in Egypt, mainland Portugal or Argentina. A drawn area is fitted live in your browser.
  • Read the verdict in plain words: is this month or season normal here, and how does it rank among 26 years.
  • See the fire calendar (years by months), the typical year and its critical period, the busiest months and years, and unusual seasons.
  • Pick any day and see that day's fires from MODIS and VIIRS on NASA satellite imagery, with how that week and month compare with normal.
  • Download the hotspots and the harmonized record as CSV, the calendar as an image, or a one-page season brief.

What the record shows

Only a record that crosses 2012 in one unit can show this. In the Nile Delta, burning seen from space did not fall after Egypt's 2004 burning ban: it rose 97% by 2005 to 2011 (the record cannot say what the ban itself did). Since 2018 it has been about half its earlier level (53% lower), with 2023 the one exception. The 2026 season is preliminary data.

Who it is for

Early-warning and emergency teams, like the CONAE team behind this challenge, who need to know whether a fire season is unusual while they wait for imagery; environmental agencies checking whether a policy changed burning; scientists, journalists and land managers who need trends that cross the 2012 break.

What makes it different

FIRMS shows the two records side by side. Zij joins them, states how sure it is, refuses to convert where the data is too thin, and is small enough to calibrate a user's own area in the browser.

Roro's Fire Diary: the game

zij.watch/diary is a short game that shows how Zij works, in five levels on the real record of the Nile Delta, with Roro the hoopoe and two satellites: Spot, Sort, Count, Translate and Compare. Its numbers come from Zij's own data files, and each level has a one-sentence note for grown-ups.

Limits

The unit counts places and days with fire, not burned area or the size of one fire. Satellites see only what burns as they pass; clouds and smoke hide fires. The record covers three countries today. The newest weeks are near-real-time data, and FIRMS revises them.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, Next.js, TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, Terra Draw, Radix UI. Hosted on Vercel; code under Apache-2.0 at github.com/zij-watch/zij.

Team

Five people, one part each: a lead developer (data pipeline, model and app), a designer (interface, map and film), a researcher (validation against FIRMS and the literature), a tester (areas, devices and the demo), and a coordinator (documentation and submission).

Prepared before the event

Research, method decisions and the design system were prepared before the event, and the public FIRMS files were downloaded in advance. The README lists exactly what.

Use of AI

Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) were our main AI tools: they wrote and reviewed code for the data pipeline, the model fitting and the web app, and helped draft the documentation. Manus AI helped build part of the game Roro's Fire Diary. No AI image, video or voice generators were used: the voice-over is a team member's own voice, and every number comes from code run on NASA FIRMS data.
